concept.name: Quorum Consistency & Raft Consensus
concept.tagline: Guarantee strong consistency across distributed database nodes using Quorum math (R + W > N) and Raft leader election.

spark.summary: Data replication copies datasets across multiple network nodes to ensure high availability, read scalability, and disaster fault tolerance. Managing replicas forces architects to navigate the fundamental trade-off between strong consistency (immediate linearizability) and high availability during network partitions (CAP and PACELC Theorems).
spark.keyTakeaway: Select your replication topology deliberately: Single-Leader (Raft/Paxos) guarantees strict serializability at the expense of write downtime during leader failover; Leaderless (Dynamo/Cassandra) maximizes write availability through Quorums (R + W > N) and eventual consistency.

concept.whyItMatters: Single database instances inevitably experience hardware failures, power outages, and routine maintenance. Without replication, a hardware crash causes permanent data loss and customer downtime. With replication, systems survive node crashes seamlessly.
whenToUse: Building fault-tolerant systems that survive hardware failure without data loss or downtime.
Scaling read-heavy applications by distributing read queries across multiple read replicas.
Multi-region global deployments providing low-latency reads close to international users.
Disaster recovery planning with cross-datacenter asynchronous replication standby pairs.
whenNotToUse: Ephemeral scratch caches or temporary worker queues where lost data can simply be recomputed.
Single-instance edge devices or embedded IoT microcontrollers with limited storage and network connectivity.
keyPoints: Single-Leader Replication: All writes route to a designated leader, which streams change logs to followers. Simple consistency model, but the leader is a write bottleneck and failover introduces downtime.
Leaderless Replication: Clients write to and read from multiple replica nodes concurrently. Governed by Quorum arithmetic: $R + W > N$.

Synchronous vs Asynchronous Replication: Synchronous replication guarantees zero data loss ($RPO=0$) at the cost of high write latency. Asynchronous replication delivers sub-millisecond writes, but risks data loss during ungraceful leader crashes.
Replication Lag Anomalies: Asynchronous follower lag causes read-after-write inconsistencies (users submit a comment, refresh, and do not see their comment).
Quorum Tuning: In an $N=3$ cluster, setting $W=2, R=2$ guarantees that the read set and write set overlap by at least one node holding the newest version.

examples.title: Read-Your-Own-Writes Guarantee
examples.scenario: A social network user updates their profile avatar and immediately refreshes their feed.
examples.outcome: Routing user profile reads to the primary leader for 10 seconds post-write guarantees fresh data while normal feed reads route to replicas.

examples.title: Leaderless Quorum Resiliency
examples.scenario: A distributed Cassandra cluster replicates data across $N=3$ nodes with $W=2, R=2$.
examples.outcome: Even when one physical database node crashes, read and write operations continue without downtime or data corruption.

tradeOffs.pro: Single-Leader eliminates write conflicts and provides clean linearizable execution.
tradeOffs.con: Single-Leader halts all write operations during network partitions or leader re-election (CP mode).

tradeOffs.pro: Synchronous replication guarantees zero data loss (RPO = 0) and identical replica states.
tradeOffs.con: Synchronous replication blocks write threads if a single follower experiences network lag or slow disk I/O.

tradeOffs.factor: Quorum Overlap ($R+W > N$) vs Eventual Consistency
tradeOffs.pro: Quorum consistency guarantees clients read the latest acknowledged write.
tradeOffs.con: Quorum reads require multiple network hops and resolve conflicts via vector clocks or last-write-wins.

failureModes.name: Split-Brain Leader Collision
failureModes.description: A network partition divides a 5-node cluster into groups of 2 and 3. The 2-node minority elects a rogue leader while the 3-node majority continues, causing diverging data writes.
failureModes.mitigation: Require a strict majority quorum ($Q = \lfloor N/2 \rfloor + 1$) for leader elections and writes, preventing minority partitions from accepting writes.

failureModes.name: Replication Lag Ghost Reads
failureModes.description: A follower falls 5 seconds behind the leader due to an intensive backup snapshot. Clients reading from this follower see stale historical records and report phantom data rollbacks.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement monotonic reads and monitor replication lag metrics (e.g. Postgres pg_stat_replication), temporarily evicting followers with lag exceeding 1 second.

failureModes.name: Last-Write-Wins (LWW) Data Silent Erasure
failureModes.description: In a leaderless system, two writes occur at the same millisecond. Clocks drift between nodes by 10ms, causing an earlier write with an advanced clock to overwrite a later write.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Vector Clocks or Lamport Timestamps to detect true causal concurrency rather than relying on unsynchronized physical wall clocks.

commonMistakes: Assuming $R + W > N$ eliminates all concurrency anomalies without accounting for concurrent overlapping writes.
Failing to monitor replica lag, allowing followers to fall hours behind until disk space exhausts.
Not testing automated failover under realistic chaos conditions, discovering split-brain bugs during live outages.

deepDive.markdownContent:
## 📖 Operational Architecture of Distributed Replication

Replication copies data across physically separate nodes to ensure data survives hardware destruction and network outages. The central challenge of distributed replication is coordinating concurrent mutations across unbonded, asynchronous network channels.

```architecture
{
  "view": "high-level",
  "title": "Single-Leader vs Leaderless Quorum Replication Models",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "client", "label": "Client Application", "type": "client" },
    { "id": "leader", "label": "Primary Leader (Accepts Writes)", "type": "database" },
    { "id": "follower1", "label": "Follower Replica 1 (Sync WAL Stream)", "type": "database" },
    { "id": "follower2", "label": "Follower Replica 2 (Async WAL Stream)", "type": "database" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "client", "to": "leader", "label": "WRITE user_id=9482 (SQL / Mutation)" },
    { "from": "leader", "to": "follower1", "label": "Sync Append to WAL (Wait for ACK)" },
    { "from": "leader", "to": "follower2", "label": "Async Stream to WAL (Fire-and-forget)" },
    { "from": "follower1", "to": "leader", "label": "Acknowledge Flush" },
    { "from": "leader", "to": "client", "label": "Commit Acknowledged" }
  ]
}
```

---

### ⚙️ Quorum Arithmetic in Practice

In leaderless replication (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Amazon S3), consistency is governed by three variables:
- $N$: The replication factor (number of nodes storing a copy of the key).
- $W$: The write quorum (number of nodes that must acknowledge a write before success).
- $R$: The read quorum (number of nodes that must respond to a read before returning).

$$\mathbf{R + W > N} \implies \text{Read and Write Quorum Sets MUST Overlap!}$$

If an $N=3$ cluster is configured with $W=2$ and $R=2$:
- $R + W = 4 > 3$.
- At least one node in the read quorum is mathematically guaranteed to be part of the write quorum that accepted the latest mutation.

questions.title: Quorum Intersection Mathematical Guarantee
questions.prompt: In a distributed cluster of N=5 nodes, why does setting Read Quorum R=3 and Write Quorum W=3 guarantee strong consistency for all read queries?

options.text: Because 5 is a prime number.
options.explanation: Prime numbers are irrelevant to quorum intersection math.

options.text: Because R + W = 6 > 5 (N), ensuring at least one node in any read quorum set of 3 nodes overlaps with the latest write quorum set of 3 nodes.
options.explanation: Correct! Pigeonhole principle guarantees R + W > N sets intersect.

rubric.excellent: Cites R + W > N formula and explains set intersection guarantee.
rubric.gap: Confuses quorum with single-leader master-slave.

questions.sampleSolution: R + W (3 + 3 = 6) exceeds total nodes N=5. By the pigeonhole principle, any read quorum of 3 nodes must include at least one node from the write quorum.
questions.explanation: Set intersection math ensures stale reads are impossible when R + W > N.

interviewProblems.title: Global Multi-Region Distributed Key-Value Store
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are designing etcd for a global Kubernetes cluster spanning 5 cloud regions. During a cross-continent fiber cut, the cluster partitions into 2 nodes (Region A, B) and 3 nodes (Region C, D, E). How does your consensus protocol prevent split-brain data corruption?
constraints: Network partition isolates 2 nodes from 3 nodes.

dimensions.name: Majority Quorum Enforcement
dimensions.description: Requiring > N/2 (3 of 5) votes for Raft leader election and write commits.

dimensions.name: Minority Partition Behavior
dimensions.description: Rejecting writes on the 2-node minority partition.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Raft requires majority consensus (> N/2 = 3 nodes). The 3-node partition achieves majority (3/5), elects a leader, and accepts writes. The 2-node minority partition fails to reach quorum and steps down to read-only/error mode, preventing split-brain.
commonPitfalls: Allowing both sides of a network partition to accept writes.
